newsitem.title: GERMANY: Stage set for heathly Daimler future - Schrempp.
newsitem.headline: Stage set for heathly Daimler future - Schrempp.

text.p: A sweeping reorganisation of Daimler-Benz AG has left the industrial giant poised to enjoy healthy growth for the next decade, chairman Juergen Schrempp said on Thursday.

Speaking to a group of investors, Schrempp said Daimler, once top-heavy with managers and known for slow decision making, has finally developed a structure that will enable it to nimbly compete on the international stage.
"We have all the formal preconditions in place to make the company healthy for the next 10 years," Schrempp said. "The next step is to enact our goals."

Spearheaded by Schrempp, Daimler undertook a massive restructuring in January, slashing layers of middle management and, most importantly, legally killing its Mercedes-Benz unit, melting it into the corporate structure.

Schrempp told the investors that the move has cut the time it takes to approve things like budgets to four months from eight to 10 months in the past and was crucial to making the company competitive.
He said due to the overhaul, Daimler was able to conclude its purchase of Ford Motor Co's heavy truck business in a matter of weeks rather than the months it would have taken under the old structure.
Schrempp denied, however, that his emphasis on improving shareholder value was leading to decisions geared largely to making quick profits.

A member of Daimler's management board said earlier this month in Geneva that the company would report group net profit of more than two billion marks, a sharp recovery from 1996's record 5.7 billion mark loss.
"We are seeing medium to long-term growth without forgetting short-term profitability," he said.
Although profits may be climbing, the Daimler chief said the company's work was not done yet.
"We are only half way there," he said. "We have to lift the quality of the workforce, especially at the management level."

Fighting to improve the workforce, however, has earned Schrempp a reputation as a ruthless cost-cutter who was laying siege to Germany's consensus-based decision making processs - where unions work closely with businesses to decide things like pay raises and changes to working conditions.
While saying that German business leaders needed to stand up for themselves against unions, he said he still supported the consensus-based model.
"Consensus means a constructive fight to find the optimal solution," he said.
And only by becoming more flexible will German jobs be preserved he said, noting that Daimler has added jobs in several plants where innovative labour contracts have been agreed.
